extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and empirically-minded inquiry (scientists, historians, legal fact-finders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and avoiding common fallacies in observation, induction, and inference (non‑observation, mal‑observation, and bad generalization) when forming or evaluating empirical and philosophical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑observation — Overlooking instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑observation occurs when errors consist in overlooking or neglecting facts or particulars which ought to have been observed (instances omitted from consideration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize from a biased set of remembered or reported cases; actively seek contrary or negative instances (Elimination of Chance). Examples: undue credit to fortune‑tellers or almanac predictions because fulfilled instances are remembered while failures are forgotten. When judging a hypothesis, collect instances on both sides rather than relying on the memorable positives alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑observation — Overlooking circumstances of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑observation may take the form of overlooking material circumstances of particular instances that would alter their evidential weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a purported instance, investigate surrounding conditions that might explain the result (collusion, hidden interventions, concurrent causes). Examples: apparent fulfilled prophecies explained by collusion; medical cures attributed to a remedy that coincided with rest/regimen or other treatments. Failure to note such circumstances vitiates inductive inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceived opinion as cause of non‑observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A preconceived theory or belief often prevents observation of facts contrary to the received tenet; observers notice only what confirms their starting view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to the powerful tendency of prior beliefs to filter perception and memory. Remedy: perform simple decisive experiments or tests rather than relying on impression or authority. Historical examples: the Copernican objections that could have been settled by experiment; travelers’ reports that only confirm prior expectations; historians seeing only what favors their party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias toward affirmative instances (affirmatives over negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human intellect is more moved by affirmative instances than by negatives, even though negative instances are often more valuable in forming sound axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give due weight to negative evidence; in constructing axioms or laws, prioritize negative instances (instances that disprove alternatives) as they have greater discriminating power. Beware collectors of anecdotes who accumulate confirming stories while ignoring disconfirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mal‑observation — Mistaking inference for perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Mal‑observation occurs when something seen is seen wrongly — specifically when what is inference or conjecture is taken and reported as direct perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish explicitly between what was directly perceived and what is inferred from perception. Examples: apparent sunrise/sunset 'seen' as proof the sun moves (Copernican resistance); witnesses who narrate impressions or inferences as facts. In testimony and description, require delineation of perception versus conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion in description: mixing observation and hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In the act of observation and in transmitting descriptions, inference and perception are often blended so that reports contain theoretical language presented as straightforward fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to separate raw sensory report from theoretical interpretation; skilled observers (e.g., painters, trained clinicians) practice this analytic discrimination. When writing or testifying, mark which elements are direct sensory data and which are interpretive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete empirical accounting (hidden or unmeasured products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent empirical facts can be wrongly taken as supporting a theory when important parts of the phenomena are unobserved or unmeasured (e.g., gaseous products of combustion overlooked in phlogiston theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure experimental inquiry accounts for all relevant products and variables (including non‑obvious or non‑solid residues). Avoid forming or clinging to hypotheses that succeed only because crucial evidence was not sought or noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution error from simultaneous interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing an effect to a single agent while other remedial actions or natural processes (rest, regimen, bandaging, etc.) were also in play leads to false causal attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causal claims (especially cures), control for or at least record concurrent treatments and natural history. Examples: sympathetic powder credited while wound healing was due to bandaging; John Wesley attributing recovery to a plaster but rest/regimen likely key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing a part for the whole (partial observation fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers may see and reason from the immediate, concentrated, obvious portion of an effect and neglect widely diffused or longer‑term consequences, thus mistaking part for whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the full chain of consequences (including dispersed, delayed, and indirect effects) rather than assuming visible immediate outcomes exhaust the effect. Examples: apparent employment from lavish spending vs. employment sustained by saving/investment; the free‑trade objection that confuses visible local gains with overall value flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking an observed appearance for proof of a theoretical fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearances compatible with multiple theories are sometimes treated as incontrovertible sensory proof of one theory rather than as data requiring interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that perceptions are appearances and may be equally compatible with alternative explanations; avoid treating appearance as decisive proof. Example: people 'saw' the sun rise and inferred the sun's motion, whereas what was seen were appearances compatible with both geocentric and heliocentric accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness and testimonial unreliability due to inference‑laden reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators and witnesses often embed hypotheses and conjectures in their reports, making their testimony unreliable unless these are separated from direct perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cross‑examination and evidence assessment, extract the pure perceptual report and treat inferential elements separately; give less weight to reports that cannot be disentangled from hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization — wrong conception of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors of generalization arise when the legitimate mode of drawing conclusions from observation and experiment is fundamentally misconceived; such generalizations are groundless if they contravene the principles of well‑grounded induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the established rules of induction (seek decisive instances, consider negative instances, account for confounding circumstances) when generalizing. Distinguish casual lapses from principled fallacies: the latter rest on erroneous theory of induction and require conceptual correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of empirical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are kinds of generalization which experience cannot provide the necessary conditions to establish by correct induction; some propositions cannot be proved by empirical enumeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the epistemic limits of observation and experiment; do not demand that experience can establish every generalization, and be wary of attempting to extend induction beyond what data can warrant.
